constraints.text: Principle II: a summary of part of an article must be distinguishable from a summary of the whole.
A content item that failed and one that produced a result must be distinguishable in storage; today the oversized item is never stored at all and is retried every cycle.

The kind classifier bounds its request 'regardless of the source content's length, so the request is about the same size for a 3-line RSS blurb and a 700k-character page': bounding, not refusing, is the existing precedent.

Measured 2026-10-07: https://ascii.rest/ extracts to 1,037,842 characters / 1,724,631 UTF-8 bytes (497,171 non-ASCII characters) and was refused at 482,792 tokens against a 400,000-token window: about 2.15 characters or 3.57 bytes per token.
Measured on cerebro's 39,022 stored items: the largest is 790,301 UTF-8 bytes (785,911 characters), all 12 items over 259k characters carry a summary, and 8 exceed 350,000 bytes.
Both production services (cerebro ~/.config/llm-core/services.toml, prismis-light and prismis-deep) run openai/gpt-5.4-nano, a 400,000-token window; services.toml records no context-window size.

A byte-level BPE token always encodes at least one byte, so a prompt's token count never exceeds its UTF-8 byte count: a byte bound under the window guarantees a fit for any text, while a character bound guarantees nothing for text that tokenizes below one character per token.

reuse.what: the existing request caps, the pattern for bounding a prompt by content size
`build_llm_analysis`, where the analysis JSON already records per-item fetch facts

open: Is the bound sized to guarantee a fit (UTF-8 bytes, since a BPE token always covers at least one byte, set under the 400,000-token window, which also cuts the tails of the 12 stored book-length pages between 259k and 786k characters that fit today), or sized to ordinary prose (characters, about a million, which leaves those 12 whole but can still overflow on pages like ascii.rest)?
